title: Genesis Mission
summary:
Genesis was a NASA sample-return probe that collected a sample of solar wind particles and returned them to Earth for analysis. It was a Discovery-class mission of the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology. The spacecraft was designed and built by Lockheed Martin Space Systems at a total mission cost of US$264 million.

NASA launched the craft on a Delta II 7326 rocket on August 8, 2001. It was the first NASA sample-return mission to return material since the Apollo program, and the first to return material from beyond the orbit of the Moon. Genesis cruised to the Earth-Sun L1 Lagrange point and entered an elliptical orbit on November 16, 2001. Genesis exposed its collector arrays and began collecting solar wind particles, a process that lasted 850 days ending on April 1, 2004.

The sample return capsule crash-landed in Utah on September 8, 2004, after a design flaw prevented the deployment of its drogue parachute. The proximate cause was that G-switch sensors were in an inverted orientation per an erroneous design and were unable to sense deceleration during atmospheric entry to initiate parachute deployment.

Despite the crash, the mission was ultimately considered a success. Although most collectors were damaged, some were successfully recovered. The Genesis science team demonstrated that contamination could be removed or avoided and solar wind particles could be analyzed. The main result concerns oxygen isotopes: the Sun is more enriched in oxygen-16 than rocky solar system bodies, suggesting oxygen-16 was somehow depleted as inner solar system materials were forming.
